# Brake Pads Finished on Only 1 Front Wheel

Uneven brake pad wear is a classic symptom of hydraulic imbalance or mechanical binding, and it rarely resolves itself once the pads are fully depleted. When you discover that one pair of pads is completely gone while its counterpart across the axle still has significant life remaining, the issue isn't simply "wear"; it's a failure of the system to distribute pressure equally. In your specific case, where the brake job was performed at a reputable shop like Midas back in February and screeching returned just two days later with catastrophic wear on one side, the culprit is almost certainly an air pocket trapped in the caliper or a seized slide pin preventing the piston from retraction.

The physics here are straightforward but often misunderstood by owners who might assume the brake fluid is clean. When you replace pads at a shop, the caliper pistons extend to clear the new friction material. As that fluid expands during the bleeding process, it pushes air back into the system if the bleeder valve isn't cycled correctly or if the master cylinder reservoir drops too low. That tiny bubble acts as a sponge; when you press the pedal, the fluid compresses rather than moving the piston with full force. On the affected wheel, the caliper effectively "floats" on that air pocket. The result is that one pad grabs while the other sits idle, creating an uneven load distribution that grinds the remaining material away in seconds.

You mentioned screeching shortly after the change. This high-pitched noise usually indicates metal-on-metal contact because the backing plate has exposed itself as the pad wears down to zero thickness on that specific wheel. If you inspected the caliper and found the pads finished while the other side remains full, the hydraulic circuit for that wheel is compromised. The most probable cause is a leak at the bleeder valve or a master cylinder failure where air was drawn back in after the job was completed.

### Diagnosing the Mechanical Bind

Before assuming a fluid issue, you must rule out mechanical binding. Brake calipers are designed to slide freely on their guide pins to allow for even pad wear and proper piston retraction. If those pins are corroded or lack fresh lubrication, the caliper cannot move laterally. When you apply brakes, one side of the pad might clamp down while the other drags or fails to engage due to friction against the bracket. Over time, this uneven force can lead to premature wear on one side even if the hydraulic pressure is nominal.

To verify this, remove the caliper and inspect the slide pins. If they are seized, replace them with new ones and apply high-temperature silicone greaseânot general-purpose lithium grease, which attracts dust and hardens quickly. A common mistake technicians make is reusing old pins or using the wrong lubricant, leading to exactly the scenario you described: uneven wear returning days after service.

### The Bleeding Process Nuances

If the mechanical components check out, the issue lies in the bleeding procedure. Standard bleeding protocols often fail if the reservoir isn't kept topped off throughout the process. As air pockets form and are pushed toward the master cylinder, they can enter the reservoir, creating a vortex that pulls more air into the system. This is why many professional shops use a vacuum bleeder or pressure bled system rather than manual pedal pumping alone.

If you attempt to bleed this yourself without proper equipment, ensure you do not let the fluid level drop below the minimum mark on the master cylinder reservoir. Once air enters the brake lines, it mixes with the hydraulic fluid. Since air is compressible and fluid is incompressible, a system contaminated with air will feel spongy and fail to transmit force evenly. The wheel with the finished pads indicates that the pressure was insufficient to hold both pads against the rotor simultaneously, causing rapid wear on one side while the other remained untouched.

### Preventive Measures for Future Service

To prevent recurrence, always inspect the brake fluid condition during any pad replacement. Fluid older than two years or showing signs of moisture contamination should be flushed entirely, regardless of mileage. Moisture in the fluid lowers its boiling point, leading to vapor lock under heavy braking, which mimics air in the lines and causes uneven braking performance.

Additionally, ensure the caliper pistons are cleaned and lubricated before reassembly. Some manufacturers recommend specific cleaning agents to remove old rubber seals that might have hardened and prevented full piston extension or retraction. If the seals were not replaced during your pad change, they may have been damaged by debris introduced during installation, leading to internal leakage that mimics an air lock.

Finally, verify the torque specifications on all caliper bolts. An overtightened bracket can distort the mounting points, inducing drag and uneven wear patterns similar to a seized slide pin. Always cross-reference the vehicle's service manual for exact torque values, as over-torquing is a frequent error that leads to premature brake failure. Addressing these factors ensures balanced braking performance and extends the life of your new pads significantly.
